blocks.text: Given an array of positive integers arr and an integer target, find two non-overlapping (no shared indices) contiguous subarrays, each summing exactly to target, minimizing the sum of their two lengths. Return this minimum sum of lengths, or -1 if no such pair of subarrays exists.

blocks.text: Given a positive-integer array arr and a target sum, find two non-overlapping contiguous subarrays that both sum exactly to target, minimizing the total combined length of the two, or determine that no such pair exists.

blocks.title: Analogy: Splitting a Grocery Bill Into Two Separate Receipts
blocks.text: Like scanning a long grocery receipt looking for two separate, non-overlapping runs of items that each add up to exactly a target amount, and wanting the two shortest such runs combined. As each qualifying run is found while scanning left to right, remembering the shortest run seen so far (up to just before where the newest run begins) lets a fresh combination be checked instantly, without ever re-scanning earlier parts of the receipt.

blocks.text: Edge case: no two non-overlapping matches exist
If fewer than two non-overlapping subarrays summing to target can be found anywhere in arr (even if one or more individual matches exist), the answer is -1.
Before checking every possible pair of matching subarrays against each other, notice that once matches are found scanning left to right, only the SHORTEST match seen so far ever needs remembering.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Since every value in arr is positive, a sliding window's sum only ever grows as it grows and shrinks as it shrinks, so a standard variable-size sliding window (grow, then shrink while sum exceeds target) finds every subarray summing exactly to target in a single linear pass.

Observation 2: When a match [left, right] is found, any earlier match that ends before left (non-overlapping) could combine with it; among all such earlier matches, only the SHORTEST one ever matters, since a shorter combined length is always at least as good.

Observation 3: Maintaining a running array bestEndingAtOrBefore[i], holding the shortest match found anywhere from the very start up through index i, lets "the best non-overlapping match to my left" be looked up in O(1) the moment a new match is found.

Observation 4: Every time a new match [left, right] completes, check bestEndingAtOrBefore[left - 1] (if it exists) and combine it with the new match's length, updating the overall answer; then update bestEndingAtOrBefore[right] with the running best.

Recognizing that only a single running "best-so-far" value (not every individual earlier match) is ever needed to check for a valid combination collapses an apparently quadratic pairing search into one linear pass.

This is a variable-size sliding window (for finding target-sum matches) paired with a running "best value seen so far" array (mirroring Kadane's running-value philosophy), enabling instant combination checks as new matches are discovered.
First find every subarray summing to target directly, then check every pair of matches for non-overlap, tracking the minimum combined length.

items: For every possible starting index, walk forward, recording every (start, end) pair whose sum equals target.
For every pair of recorded matches, check whether they overlap; if not, track the minimum combined length among all non-overlapping pairs.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every matching subarray is recorded first, in a single O(n squared) pass, since the combination step needs the full list of matches to compare against each other.
The overlap check (e1 < s2 or e2 < s1) directly tests whether one match ends entirely before the other begins, in either order.
best only ever decreases, tracking the minimum combined length across every valid non-overlapping pair.

blocks.text: Every possible matching subarray is found, and every pair of matches is checked for overlap, so the correct minimum combined length is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared) to find every match, plus O(k squared) to compare every pair of the k matches found, which can itself be O(n squared) in the worst case.
Space: O(k) for storing the matches, up to O(n) in the worst case.

Limitation: comparing every pair of matches against each other ignores that, scanning matches in left-to-right order, only the single shortest earlier match ever needs to be remembered and combined with each new match found.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force compares every pair of matches. Instead, use a single variable-size sliding window to find every target-sum match in one linear pass (valid since all values are positive). Alongside it, maintain a running array bestEndingAtOrBefore, where bestEndingAtOrBefore[i] holds the shortest match found anywhere up through index i. Every time a new match completes, look up bestEndingAtOrBefore just before that match's start, combine it with the new match's length if it exists, and update the answer; then update the running array with the new match's length if it improves things.

Slide a variable-size window across arr, growing right and shrinking left whenever the sum exceeds target. Whenever the sum equals target exactly, compute the match's length, check bestEndingAtOrBefore[left - 1] for a combinable earlier match, and update the running best. After processing each position, update bestEndingAtOrBefore at that index with the current running best.
Slide a single variable-size window for target-sum matches, combining each new match with the best non-overlapping match found so far.

codes.python:
def min_sum_of_lengths(arr, target):
    n = len(arr)
    best_ending_at_or_before = [float('inf')] * n                          # shortest valid subarray ending anywhere from 0 up to this index
    left = 0
    total = 0
    running_best = float('inf')
    answer = float('inf')
    for right in range(n):
        total += arr[right]
        while total > target:                                             # all values are positive, so shrinking only ever decreases the sum
            total -= arr[left]
            left += 1
        if total == target:
            length = right - left + 1
            if left > 0 and best_ending_at_or_before[left - 1] != float('inf'):
                answer = min(answer, best_ending_at_or_before[left - 1] + length)   # combine with the best NON-OVERLAPPING match found so far
            running_best = min(running_best, length)
        best_ending_at_or_before[right] = running_best
    return answer if answer != float('inf') else -1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(min_sum_of_lengths([3, 2, 2, 4, 3], 3))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), since left and right each advance forward at most n times total, and the combination lookup is O(1) per match.
Space: O(n) for the bestEndingAtOrBefore array.

Because all values are positive, the standard variable-size sliding window correctly finds every subarray summing exactly to target in one linear pass. Since bestEndingAtOrBefore[i] always holds the shortest match ending anywhere from the start through index i, looking it up at (left - 1) the moment a new match [left, right] is found instantly retrieves the best possible NON-OVERLAPPING partner for that match, without ever needing to compare against every individual earlier match directly.

items: bestEndingAtOrBefore is built incrementally, always reflecting the shortest match found up through (and including) the current index.
The combination check only triggers when left > 0, since a match starting at index 0 has no room for an earlier, non-overlapping match at all.
runningBest is updated only when a strictly shorter match is found, always representing the best single match seen so far, ready for the next combination check.

blocks.text: Tracking a single running "best match so far" value (rather than every individual match) to combine with each newly found match is the same underlying philosophy as Kadane's Algorithm, applied here to enable instant non-overlapping combination checks.

items: Comparing every pair of matches against each other directly, instead of recognizing that only the single best (shortest) earlier match ever needs remembering.
Looking up bestEndingAtOrBefore at the wrong index (e.g., at "left" instead of "left - 1"), which could incorrectly allow the two chosen subarrays to overlap by one position.

Forgetting that all values must be positive for the standard variable-size sliding window to correctly find every target-sum match; with negative values present, a different technique (e.g., prefix sums with a hash map) would be needed instead.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find two non-overlapping subarrays matching some condition, minimizing a combined property" points toward finding matches with a sliding window (or similar single-pass technique) while maintaining a running "best match found so far" value, enabling O(1) combination checks as new matches are discovered.

items: How would this extend to finding THREE non-overlapping subarrays instead of two? A second running array, tracking "best combined length of 2 non-overlapping matches ending at or before index i", would need to be built and combined with newly found matches, generalizing the same technique.

What if arr could contain negative numbers? The standard variable-size sliding window would no longer correctly find every target-sum match; a prefix-sum-based approach with a hash map (tracking earliest/shortest matches per prefix sum) would be needed instead.

How would you also report the actual two subarrays, not just their combined length? Track the (start, end) indices alongside the length in bestEndingAtOrBefore, and record both matches' indices whenever the answer improves.

Combines the variable-size sliding window technique (for finding target-sum matches, as in Minimum Size Subarray Sum) with a running "best value so far" array in the spirit of Kadane's Algorithm, enabling efficient non-overlapping combination checks.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) or worse time, O(n) space.
Optimized (sliding window + running best-so-far array): O(n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Variable-size sliding window (for target-sum matches) combined with a running "best match so far" array
Core Idea: Every time a new target-sum match is found, instantly combine it with the shortest non-overlapping match found so far, tracked via a running array
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: Only the single best (shortest) earlier match ever needs remembering, not every individual match, to check for valid combinations
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Slide for target-sum matches; combine each with bestEndingAtOrBefore[left - 1]
